identity.title: ImageNet-trained CNNs are not biased towards texture: Revisiting feature reliance through controlled suppression

problem.claim: The paper examines whether CNNs are inherently biased toward texture and how models rely on shape, texture, and color cues.

gap.claim: The authors identify limitations in the cue-conflict experiment used to study this hypothesis, including confounds from forced-choice conflicts.

contributions.claim: A domain-agnostic framework quantifies feature reliance by systematically suppressing shape, texture, and color cues.
Across controlled suppression conditions, the authors report that CNNs predominantly rely on local shape features rather than being inherently texture-biased.
The analysis spans computer vision, medical imaging, and remote sensing, reporting domain-specific reliance patterns.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish their approach by measuring feature reliance through controlled cue suppression while avoiding forced-choice conflict confounds.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that humans and neural networks evaluated under controlled suppression show CNNs are not inherently texture-biased and predominantly use local shape features.
The authors report that modern training strategies or architectures, including ConvNeXt and ViTs, can substantially mitigate this reliance.
The authors report systematic cross-domain differences: shape is prioritized in computer vision, color in medical imaging, and texture more strongly in remote sensing.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper revisits the influential hypothesis that CNNs are inherently texture-biased.
It examines limitations in the prior cue-conflict experiment.
It introduces controlled suppression of shape, texture, and color cues as a domain-agnostic measurement framework.
Controlled evaluations yield predominantly local-shape reliance for CNNs, with mitigation through modern strategies or architectures.
The analysis compares reliance patterns across computer vision, medical imaging, and remote sensing.

source_observation.claim: The paper replaces forced-choice cue conflicts with systematic suppression of individual cues to quantify feature reliance.

lessons.interpretation: Separating cues experimentally can make a feature-use claim more directly interpretable.
lessons.application: When a comparison forces competing cues into one decision, design ablations that suppress each cue independently and report the resulting reliance changes.
lessons.exception: This approach may be unsuitable when cue suppression destroys realism or removes information that is inseparable from the target task.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify suppression procedures, datasets, metrics, sample sizes, or quantitative effect sizes.
The conditions and magnitude of mitigation by training strategies, ConvNeXt, and ViTs are unspecified.
The abstract does not provide details of the code release beyond its URL.
